# Introduction {#sec-introduction}

The Norwegian WHO Labour Care Trial (NORWELCG) is a pivotal multicenter, stepped wedge cluster
randomised trial aimed at evaluating the implementation of the Labour Care Guide (LCG) compared to
the traditional WHO partograph in Norwegian hospitals. This study seeks to assess the effects of LCG
on intrapartum interventions, maternal and neonatal outcomes, and healthcare provider and patient
experiences.

The trial adopts the principles established in the ICH E9 Statistical Principles for Clinical Trials
and its addendum E9 (R1) focusing on estimands and sensitivity analyses. This SAP will elucidate the
statistical methodologies intended for estimating treatment effects, aligning the analysis with the
outlined estimands, thus ensuring a robust interpretation of trial objectives.

Protocol Changes: The SAP reflects the original design of the trial as detailed in protocol version
1.06 (dated 2024.05.09). There are currently no changes to protocol-planned analyses; future
amendments will be meticulously documented in Section 10, underscoring transparent methodological
evolutions responsive to trial conduct.

Exclusions and Supplementary Documentation: While primary and secondary analysis specifications are
contained herein, non-key analyses such as baseline summaries, exploratory endpoints, and detailed
demographic analyses are not necessarily included. Some secondary analyses are considered for
secondary publications and are further specified in topic-specific statistical analysis plans.

## Estimands for Secondary Objectives {#sec-estimands-for-secondary-objectives}

<!-- COMMENT Maria Cecilie Stivang (2026-09-22): Se min forklaring over for hvilke kvinner som tilhører hvilken periode. [2026-09-29: treatment by documentation form] -->

All estimands for secondary objectives have the following attributes:

- The target population is adult pregnant women with a planned vaginal delivery in need of a
  partograph

- The investigational intervention is using the Labour Care Guide, once implemented, as compared to
  the WHO partograph during labour. Treatment is defined by the documentation form, which each
  hospital changed at its crossover date in the randomised schedule (@fig-design,
  @sec-analysis-sets). The 5-week transition (teaching) period in each hospital belongs to neither
  condition; women delivering during it are not part of the primary analysis set.

- Any intercurrent events, such as not complying to assigned labour guideline will be handled by the
  treatment policy strategy, i.e. treat according to assigned strategy regardless of compliance

- The principal stratum of the primary estimand (caesarean sections at ≤ 4 cm excluded,
  @sec-estimand-for-primary-objective) does not apply to the secondary endpoints: all women in the
  analysis set are included, also those with a caesarean section at 4 cm cervical dilatation
  (caesarean sections before 4 cm were not recorded in the trial). The secondary endpoints are
  assessed from 4 cm, where the WHO partograph starts; neither tool is used before 4 cm. Caesarean
  sections at 4 cm in the LCG period were registered retrospectively, because the LCG form starts
  at 5 cm; any missed cases would favour the LCG.

- For amniotomy, oxytocin and epidural analgesia, only interventions performed or started at 4 cm
  cervical dilatation or more are events, and women whose intervention was performed or started at
  ≤ 3 cm are removed from the analysis of that endpoint (@sec-definition-of-efficacy-endpoints-for):
  the estimand targets women who reach 4 cm without the intervention, a principal stratum. No
  outcome window is applied to the other endpoints.

- For endpoints that exist only after a vaginal birth (perineal support, episiotomy, perineal
  tears), a caesarean section is an intercurrent event that precludes the outcome. It is handled by
  a principal stratum strategy — the stratum of women who would deliver vaginally with either
  labour-monitoring tool — estimated in the vaginal delivery set (@sec-analysis-sets). This relies
  on the LCG not changing which women deliver vaginally. A supplementary analysis, which does not
  need this assumption, uses a composite strategy, counting a caesarean section as no event, in the
  primary analysis set.

- In time from 4 cm cervical dilatation to vaginal delivery, a caesarean section is handled by a
  composite strategy: it counts as no vaginal delivery during the whole of the first 36 hours after
  4 cm, i.e. as at least as unfavourable as the longest labours ending in a vaginal delivery
  (@sec-main-analytical-approach-for-time-to). A caesarean section is not treated as censoring,
  which would target a hypothetical setting in which caesarean section is not available.

- Population-level summary measures will be

  - Absolute and relative difference in proportion for dichotomous endpoints

  - Common odds ratio and difference in the probability of a third- or fourth-degree tear for
    degree of perineal tears

  - Difference in restricted mean time without vaginal delivery during the first 36 hours after 4 cm
    for time from 4 cm cervical dilatation to vaginal delivery

## Study Design {#sec-study-design}

From the protocol section 4: The NORWELCG will be conducted as a stepped wedge cluster randomised
trial. The choice of cluster randomisation will secure a standard guideline for the entire
department/unit as there would be a risk of contamination if randomising on an individual level,
given that the same midwife/obstetrician could care for women with different guidelines at the same
time. The choice of a stepped wedge cluster randomised design is based on the possible risk of the
Hawthorne effect in a standard cluster randomised trial, experienced when conducting the multicentre
cluster randomised trial: The Labour Progression Study in Norway 2014-2018 (17). By allowing all
units to use both the WHO partograph and the LCG in steps, the risk of bias represented by
contamination and the Hawthorne effect will be reduced to a minimum. A non-inferiority approach has
been chosen to evaluate the effect of the LCG. Labour outcomes are overall good in Norway and a
possible national enrolment of the LCG should be based on results similar (or in case better) than
we already have. The choice of intrapartum caesarean section rate as main outcome is due to its
significance and the potential to merge results with other ongoing LCG studies on research priority
questions stated by the WHO.

*Randomisation*

Prior to trial commencement, the clusters will be randomly assigned to one of the sequences (S1-S10)
for time of transition from WHO partograph to the LCG (@fig-design), using a computer-generated
randomisation system. To obtain an equal distribution of small and larger hospitals during the study
period, randomisation will be stratified by hospital size. To obtain an equal distribution of
intrapartum caesarean section rates between units, randomisation will also be stratified by the rate
of intrapartum caesarean sections prior to onset of the trial. The allocation sequence will be
masked for the units until the unit is in turn for transition to the LCG, to avoid contamination.

```{r}
#| label: fig-design
#| fig-cap: "**Overview of the study steps and transition periods.** C = Cluster, FS = feasibility study of the electronic version of the LCG. S = steps of 5 weeks (S1-S12 = 60 weeks). Green colour denotes WHO partograph period, white colour denotes transition period for and teaching period, and blue colour denotes LCG period"
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 3.4
# Stepped-wedge schedule as in the protocol Figure 1: cluster c uses the WHO
# partograph in FS 2024 and S1..Sc, is in transition in S(c+1), and uses the
# LCG from S(c+2).
library(ggplot2)
steps <- c("FS 2024", paste0("S", 1:12))
sw <- expand.grid(cluster = 1:10, s = 0:12)
sw$period <- with(sw, ifelse(s <= cluster, "WHO partograph",
                      ifelse(s == cluster + 1, "Transition", "LCG")))
sw$period <- factor(sw$period, c("WHO partograph", "Transition", "LCG"))
sw$step <- factor(sw$s, levels = 0:12, labels = steps)
sw$clus <- factor(sw$cluster, levels = 10:1)
ggplot(sw, aes(step, clus, fill = period)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "grey35", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_text(data = subset(sw, period == "Transition"), aes(label = "T"),
            size = 3) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("WHO partograph" = "#77A548",
                               "Transition" = "white", "LCG" = "#9DC3E6")) +
  scale_x_discrete(position = "top") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "C", fill = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(), legend.position = "bottom",
        axis.title.y = element_text(angle = 0, vjust = 1))
```

# General Considerations {#sec-general-considerations}

As stated in the protocol, this SAP has been written and approved prior to commencement of the
analysis and without knowledge of allocation. Amendments to plan can be done until day of data base
lock. The statistician will perform analysis blinded to the participant's guideline allocation to
assess the appropriateness and validity of the prespecified statistical analyses. This revision will
be based on a blinded look at the data, and any changes to the SAP will not be based on any
unblinded inference.

## Statistical Hypotheses and Conclusion Criteria {#sec-statistical-hypotheses-and-conclusion}

The primary hypothesis is one of non-inferiority: the WHO partograph is the standard of care and the
LCG the new approach, and a lower caesarean section rate with the LCG would be a favourable outcome,
not a failure to show equivalence. With the difference defined as the proportion of intrapartum
caesarean sections with the LCG minus that with the WHO partograph, among women with a planned
vaginal delivery (primary estimand, @sec-estimand-for-primary-objective), the null hypothesis is

- H~0~: the difference is greater than or equal to 1.5 percentage points (the LCG is inferior),

and the alternative hypothesis is

- H~1~: the difference is less than 1.5 percentage points (the LCG is non-inferior).

The non-inferiority margin is 1.5 percentage points. The null hypothesis is rejected, and the LCG
concluded non-inferior to the WHO partograph, if the upper limit of the two-sided 95% confidence
interval for the difference lies below 1.5 percentage points. This corresponds to a one-sided test
at the 2.5% significance level.

If non-inferiority is shown, superiority of the LCG is tested next, in a fixed sequence and without
adjustment of the significance level: the LCG is concluded superior (fewer intrapartum caesarean
sections) if the upper limit of the same confidence interval also lies below 0.

## Multiplicity Adjustment {#sec-multiplicity-adjustment}

The non-inferiority and superiority tests of the primary estimand form a fixed sequence
(@sec-statistical-hypotheses-and-conclusion): superiority is tested only if non-inferiority has
been shown, which keeps the overall one-sided type I error at 2.5% without adjustment. There will be
no adjustments for multiplicity for the secondary endpoints.

## Impact of Intercurrent Events Strategies {#sec-impact-of-intercurrent-events-strategies}

The treatment policy strategy implies that we are looking at the effect of intending to use the
interventional treatment (using the LCG guideline) regardless of actual implementation or compliance
to the protocol. For the primary endpoint, the principal stratum strategy restricts the comparison
to women who reach 5 cm cervical dilatation without a caesarean section
(@sec-estimand-for-primary-objective). Stratum membership is determined
during labour, not at baseline, so the causal interpretation of the difference rests on the
assumption that the allocated tool does not affect whether a woman has a caesarean section before
5 cm. This is plausible because neither tool is used before 4 cm; any departure between 4 and 5 cm,
where only the WHO partograph is in use, would bias the comparison against the LCG, i.e.
conservatively for the non-inferiority claim. Supplementary analysis 1 in
@sec-supplementary-analysis examines the choice of threshold. The secondary endpoints include the caesarean sections at 4 cm and
are assessed from 4 cm; for amniotomy, oxytocin and epidural analgesia the stratum is women who
reach 4 cm without the intervention, and for endpoints that exist only after a vaginal birth a
further principal stratum (vaginal delivery) is used (@sec-estimands-for-secondary-objectives).

## Handling of Missing Data {#sec-handling-of-missing-data}

Generally, there will be three methods to deal with missing data:

1)  Using multiple imputation where the imputation is based on a model with baseline information
    such as women's age, gestational age, hospital, treatment and time interval as fixed effects

2)  Imputing with worst outcome

3)  Ignoring missing data

The last two approaches will only be used in cases where there are very few missing data. The
precise handling of missing data will be detailed by endpoint/estimand in section 4 and 5. The
handling of missing data will be revised before database lock and final signed version of this SAP.
This revision will be based on a blinded look at the data, and any changes to the handling will not
be based on any unblinded inference.

Missing values of covariates used for adjustment are handled by the missing-indicator method
(@sec-adjustment-for-covariates).

# Analysis Sets {#sec-analysis-sets}

<!-- COMMENT Maria Cecilie Stivang (2026-09-22): Se min tidligere kommentar. [2026-09-29: treatment by documentation form] -->
<!-- COMMENT Maria Cecilie Stivang (2026-09-25): Labour progression ble tatt bort fra denne SAP i forrige møte, vi beholdt kun time from 5 cm to vaginal delivery. [2026-09-29: removed; time to vaginal delivery now from 4 cm] -->

Three analysis sets are defined. Whether a woman belongs to the control, transition or LCG period
is determined by the documentation form, which is directly linked to the change of monitoring
tool. The LCG form was taken into use at 08:00 on the hospital's crossover date in the randomised
schedule (@fig-design): women who entered active labour after that time and were documented on the
LCG form belong to the LCG period, and women already in labour and documented on the WHO partograph
form belong to the preceding period, even if they gave birth later. The WHO partograph form was
used in both the control and the transition period; the two are separated by the hospital's
transition date in the randomised schedule, from 08:00 on that date. The period is given by the
prefix of the record key (CTR, TRAN or INT).

The time interval (step) used in the models is determined by the date and time of birth. The twelve
5-week steps start at 08:00 on the Tuesdays 1 April 2025 (step 1, week 14), 6 May, 10 June, 15 July,
19 August, 23 September, 28 October and 2 December 2025, and 6 January, 10 February, 17 March and
21 April 2026 (step 12, week 17); births on the last inclusion day (26 May 2026) belong to step 12.
A woman in labour at a change of period may therefore belong to a period that differs from the
scheduled period of the step in which she gave birth.

**Full analysis set (FAS).** All women ≥ 18 years old admitted for a planned vaginal delivery in need
of a partograph at any of the participating hospitals in the period 01.04.25-26.05.26. The
participating hospitals are: Østfold Hospital Trust, University Hospital in Northern Norway, Vestre
Viken Hospital Trust: Drammen, Stavanger University Hospital, Sørlandet Hospital: Kristiansand, Oslo
University Hospital: Ullevål, Oslo University Hospital: Rikshospitalet, St. Olav University
Hospital, Akershus University Hospital and Haukeland University hospital. Women who explicitly do not
wish to participate in the trial will be excluded. The FAS includes the women delivering during the
transition periods; it is used for the analysis that includes these periods
(@sec-supplementary-analysis) and to describe the trial population and flow.

**Primary analysis set (PAS).** The FAS excluding women delivering during their hospital's
transition period (@fig-design). During the transition period staff were trained in the LCG but were
asked not to act on it until the period had ended, so these women received neither condition as
intended. Including them, as either condition, would bias the treatment effect towards no
difference, which is anti-conservative for the non-inferiority assessment. The PAS is used for the
primary analysis and for all secondary analyses unless stated otherwise.

**Vaginal delivery set (VDS).** The women in the PAS who delivered vaginally (spontaneous or
instrumental). Used for endpoints that exist only after a vaginal birth (perineal support,
episiotomy, perineal tears; see @sec-estimands-for-secondary-objectives) and for the duration
component of time from 4 cm cervical dilatation to vaginal delivery
(@sec-main-analytical-approach-for-time-to).

The principal stratum exclusion defined for the primary estimand
(@sec-estimand-for-primary-objective) is applied to the primary endpoint and its sensitivity
analyses only; the secondary analyses include the caesarean sections at 4 cm
(@sec-estimands-for-secondary-objectives).

# Analyses Supporting Primary Objective(s) {#sec-analyses-supporting-primary-objective-s}

## Primary Estimand  {#sec-primary-estimand}

The primary estimand is the absolute difference in proportion of intrapartum caesarean sections
between women with a planned vaginal delivery in need of a partograph following the LCG and the WHO
partograph

### Definition of Endpoint(s)  {#sec-definition-of-endpoint-s}

The endpoint is delivery by intrapartum caesarean section as recorded in the hospital's medical
records. For multiple births, the woman's mode of delivery is the most operative across the babies
(caesarean section, then instrumental, then spontaneous vaginal delivery), so a caesarean section
for any baby counts as an intrapartum caesarean section. A caesarean section after a failed
instrumental attempt is a caesarean section. If the mode of delivery of a second-born twin is not
recorded, that of the first-born twin is used.

### Main Analytical Approach {#sec-main-analytical-approach}

The risk difference will be estimated from a generalised linear mixed model (binomial family, logit
link) with a random intercept for cluster (hospital) and fixed effects for treatment, time interval
(step) and the covariates in @sec-adjustment-for-covariates. The marginal (population-averaged)
risks are obtained by G-computation (standardisation): for every woman in the analysis set, the
probability of an intrapartum caesarean section is predicted under the LCG and under the WHO
partograph, with her own covariates and time interval and integrating over the distribution of the
random cluster effect (Gauss–Hermite quadrature), and the predictions are averaged over all women.
The absolute risk difference (primary summary measure) is the difference between the two averaged
risks and the relative difference (supplementary) their ratio. Standard errors are obtained by the
delta method. Because the average is taken over the time intervals of the analysis set, the
estimate refers to the whole trial period.

No missing data were found for this endpoint at the blinded data review of the final data export
(9 September 2026): mode of delivery was recorded for all 36,324 women, and cervical dilatation for
every intrapartum caesarean section, so membership of the principal stratum is also fully
determined. Should the locked database nevertheless contain missing values, they will be ignored
and handled by the model (complete-case analysis).

The absolute and relative differences will be presented with two-sided 95% confidence intervals,
which also give the non-inferiority and superiority conclusions
(@sec-statistical-hypotheses-and-conclusion).

### Adjustment for covariates {#sec-adjustment-for-covariates}

<!-- COMMENT Inge Christoffer Olsen (2026-09-10): Hvordan er disse definert? [resolved 2026-09-11: birthweight percentiles dropped; covariate derivations in the Supporting Documentation] -->
<!-- COMMENT Therese Buerengen (2026-05-04): Vi fikk 2023 tall fra MFR [resolved 2026-09-11: hospital-level covariates are not used for adjustment, see below] -->

The primary model is adjusted for a short, pre-specified set of strong prognostic factors for
intrapartum caesarean section, to increase the precision of the standardised risk difference and to
protect against changes in case mix across time intervals within hospitals:

- Robson ten-group classification (the nine groups present in a planned vaginal delivery population)

- Maternal age (years)

- Maternal pre-pregnancy body mass index (kg/m^2^)

- Maternal height (cm)

- Birth weight (g; first-born twin for multiple births)

- Gestational age at birth (weeks + days)

The set was confirmed at a blinded review of the pooled data before unblinding (all study periods
combined; no treatment, time interval or hospital term in the model): Robson group, maternal
height, birth weight, maternal age, pre-pregnancy body mass index and gestational age were the
strongest predictors of intrapartum caesarean section. Education and hypertensive disorders were borderline, and country of origin (Norway vs other)
contributed little; they are not included.

Continuous covariates enter as restricted cubic splines with three knots (10th, 50th and 90th
percentiles); this is also the default for continuous covariates in the secondary analyses unless
stated otherwise for an endpoint. The Robson classification already encodes parity, previous caesarean section, onset of
labour, fetal presentation and multiple pregnancy, which are therefore not added separately; it
distinguishes only term from preterm birth, so gestational age is included as a continuous
covariate. Hospital-level characteristics (annual number of deliveries,
intrapartum caesarean section rate) and the randomisation stratification factors are constant within a hospital
and are accounted for by the random cluster effect; they are not added as covariates.

Missing covariate values are handled by the missing-indicator method: a separate "missing" category
for categorical covariates, and the median plus a missing indicator for continuous covariates, so
that no woman is excluded from the analysis because of a missing covariate. The indicator is
included only where at least ten values are missing; with fewer, the median is used without an
indicator, because an indicator for a handful of women is not estimable.

Covariate adjustment for secondary endpoints is specified for each endpoint after a blinded review
of the data (@sec-analyses-supporting-secondary-objective). The other characteristics listed in
earlier versions of this SAP (country of origin, marital status, education, smoking, snuff use, medically treated
diabetes, hypertensive disorders, sex of the baby, head circumference) are presented
in the baseline characteristics table but not used for adjustment. Amniotomy, oxytocin infusion
and epidural analgesia started before 4 cm cervical dilatation (the women concerned are excluded
from the corresponding secondary endpoint, @sec-definition-of-efficacy-endpoints-for) are also
presented in the baseline characteristics table, as are the annual number of deliveries of the
hospital, first vaginal delivery, contractions at admission and birthweight percentile, which are
not used for adjustment. Derivations are given in @sec-data-derivations.

### Sensitivity Analyses {#sec-sensitivity-analyses}

The sensitivity analyses keep the primary estimand and vary assumptions of the main analytical
approach:

1)  Unadjusted model: the model of @sec-main-analytical-approach without the covariates of
    @sec-adjustment-for-covariates (treatment, time interval and random cluster effect only).

2)  Fixed cluster effects: hospital as a fixed effect instead of a random effect, as a check on the
    random-effect assumption with ten clusters.

### Supplementary Analysis {#sec-supplementary-analysis}

<!-- COMMENT Maria Cecilie Stivang (2026-09-22): Mulig jeg misforstår noe her, men vi har ikke data på kvinner med sectio ved 1, 2 eller 3 cm. Disse ble ekskludert fra datainnsamlingen. [2026-09-29: supplementary analyses 1 and 2 were identical on these data and are merged] -->
<!-- COMMENT Maria Cecilie Stivang (2026-09-22): Skjønte ikke helt denne setningen.. Disse ble etter-registrert, data ble altså ikke samlet inn helt på samme måte som de ble gjort i kontrollperioden. Hva menes med "Before the LCG is in use"? [2026-09-29: sentence rewritten: retrospective registration] -->

The supplementary analyses target estimands that differ from the primary estimand in one
attribute. All use the model and G-computation of @sec-main-analytical-approach.

1)  Caesarean sections at 4 cm included (intercurrent-event strategy): all women in the primary
    analysis set are analysed, and caesarean sections at 4 cm are counted as events in both periods
    (no principal stratum exclusion). Caesarean sections before 4 cm were not recorded in the trial,
    so this is also the treatment policy strategy for the recorded population. In the LCG period,
    caesarean sections at 4 cm were registered retrospectively, because the LCG form starts at 5 cm
    (confirmed by the investigators, 11 and 22 September 2026); any missed cases would favour the
    LCG.

2)  Transition periods included (treatment attribute and analysis set): all women in the full
    analysis set are analysed, with the transition period handled as a control period. During the
    transition period staff were trained in the LCG but were asked not to act on it until the period
    had ended.

3)  Exposure time (treatment attribute): the effect of the LCG is allowed to depend on the time since
    the hospital started using it, with separate LCG effects for the first 5-week step after the
    transition period and for later steps (exposure-time model; Kenny et al. 2022). This examines
    whether the effect of the LCG changes as its use becomes established.

#### Main Analytical Approach for Dichotomous Efficacy Endpoints {#sec-main-analytical-approach-for}

Dichotomous endpoints are analysed as the primary endpoint (@sec-main-analytical-approach): a
generalised linear mixed model (binomial family, logit link) with a random intercept for cluster and
fixed effects for treatment, time interval and the covariates specified for the endpoint, with the
absolute and relative differences obtained by G-computation integrating over the random cluster
effect and standard errors by the delta method. Covariates are specified per endpoint after the
blinded data review (@sec-adjustment-for-covariates). Endpoints restricted to vaginal births are
analysed in the vaginal delivery set, all others in the primary analysis set (@sec-analysis-sets).
Missing data are handled as given in the "Handling of missing data" column of the endpoint tables.

The differences are presented with two-sided 95% confidence intervals, not adjusted for
multiplicity (@sec-multiplicity-adjustment). No hypothesis tests are performed and no
non-inferiority margin applies to secondary endpoints.

Covariate sets by endpoint:

- Spontaneous vaginal delivery and instrumental vaginal delivery: as for the primary endpoint
  (@sec-adjustment-for-covariates). Mode of delivery is classified as spontaneous vaginal,
  instrumental vaginal or caesarean section, so the three differences sum to zero. The difference in
  caesarean sections in the primary analysis set, including those at 4 cm, is supplementary analysis
  1 of the primary estimand (@sec-supplementary-analysis).

- Occurrence of amniotomy during labour: as for the primary endpoint.

- Use of oxytocin during labour: as for the primary endpoint.

- Use of epidural analgesia during labour: as for the primary endpoint.

- Use of medical pain relief in labour: as for the primary endpoint.

- Intermittent fetal monitoring: as for the primary endpoint.

- Continuous fetal monitoring: as for the primary endpoint.

- Occurrence of perineal support: as for the primary endpoint.

- Episiotomy: as for the primary endpoint.

- Occurrence of postpartum haemorrhage > 1000 ml: as for the primary endpoint.

- Arterial umbilical cord pH < 7.00: as for the primary endpoint.

- Apgar score < 7 at 5 minutes: as for the primary endpoint.

- Admittance to neonatal intensive care unit within 2 hours: as for the primary endpoint.

Missing values of occurrence of perineal support (not recorded for 4,014 women in the vaginal
delivery set, 11.9%, at the blinded review) are handled by multiple imputation under a
missing-at-random assumption, using fully conditional specification (chained equations) with 20
imputed datasets. The imputation model contains all variables of the analysis model (treatment,
time interval, hospital as a fixed effect and the covariates) and the auxiliary variables mode of
vaginal delivery (spontaneous, vacuum, forceps), degree of perineal tear and episiotomy; missing
values of the auxiliary variables are imputed in the same process. The analysis of
@sec-main-analytical-approach is applied to each imputed dataset, and the estimates and their
variances are combined by Rubin's rules.

Arterial umbilical cord pH was not recorded for 27.5% of the first-born babies at the blinded
review (venous pH only for 5,321 women, no cord blood gas for 4,699). The investigators consider the
missing values unrelated to the condition of the baby (missing completely at random). Multiple
imputation is used nevertheless, because it recovers information from the venous pH and remains
valid if missingness depends on the auxiliary variables. When no baby of a woman has a
measured arterial pH, the arterial pH of the first-born baby is imputed by multiple imputation under
a missing-at-random assumption (fully conditional specification with predictive mean matching, 30
imputed datasets) and dichotomised at 7.00. The imputation model contains all variables of the
analysis model (treatment, time interval, hospital as a fixed effect and the covariates) and the
auxiliary variables venous cord pH, arterial and venous base excess or deficit, Apgar scores at 1
and 5 minutes, admission to the neonatal intensive care unit within 2 hours and mode of delivery.
For multiple births with at least one measured baby, the endpoint is taken from the measured
babies. Estimates are combined by Rubin's rules. Arterial and venous pH values outside 6.5–7.8
have been referred to the data managers for checking against the source records.

#### Main Analytical Approach for Ordinal Efficacy Endpoints {#sec-main-analytical-approach-for-ordinal}

Ordinal endpoints (degree of perineal tears) are analysed with a proportional-odds (cumulative
logit) generalised linear mixed model with a random intercept for cluster and fixed effects for
treatment, time interval and the covariates of the primary endpoint
(@sec-adjustment-for-covariates). The common cumulative odds ratio is presented with a Wald 95%
confidence interval. In addition, the marginal probability of each category under the LCG and under
the WHO partograph is obtained by G-computation, integrating over the random cluster effect as in
@sec-main-analytical-approach, and the absolute difference in the probability of a third- or
fourth-degree tear (obstetric anal sphincter injury) is presented with a two-sided 95% confidence
interval (delta method).

Missing data are handled as given in the endpoint table (complete-case analysis for degree of
perineal tears).

#### Main Analytical Approach for Time to Event Efficacy Endpoints {#sec-main-analytical-approach-for-time-to}

<!-- COMMENT Maria Cecilie Stivang (2026-09-25): Siden denne SAP ikke skal inneholde progression fra en cm til neste, så skal vel dette tas bort. [2026-09-29: labour progression section removed; the labour-curve model is kept only to impute the time of reaching 4 cm] -->

Time from 4 cm cervical dilatation to vaginal delivery is analysed as the time without vaginal
delivery during the first 36 hours after 4 cm, in the primary analysis set including the caesarean
sections at 4 cm (@sec-estimands-for-secondary-objectives). For each woman, let T be the time from
4 cm to delivery (the birth of the first baby for multiple births). The analysis variable is
Y = min(T, 36 h) after a vaginal delivery (spontaneous or instrumental) and Y = 36 h after a
caesarean section, whenever it occurs. Mode of delivery is the most operative across the babies
(@sec-definition-of-endpoint-s), so a caesarean section for a second twin counts as a caesarean
section.

The mean of Y is the restricted mean time without vaginal delivery: 36 hours minus the area under
the cumulative incidence curve of vaginal delivery up to 36 hours (Andersen 2013). The summary
measure is the difference in mean Y between the LCG and the WHO partograph, in hours; negative
values favour the LCG. Caesarean section is handled by a composite strategy
(@sec-estimands-for-secondary-objectives), so the estimand is the total effect of the LCG on
reaching a vaginal delivery over time, including any effect through caesarean section (Young et al.
2020). It is not the restricted mean survival time from a Kaplan–Meier estimator with caesarean
sections censored: that targets a hypothetical setting without caesarean section and requires
caesarean section to be independent of the time a woman would have taken to deliver vaginally,
which is implausible when caesarean sections are indicated by slow progress (Andersen and Keiding
2012).

The horizon of 36 hours is longer than virtually all times to vaginal delivery (at the blinded
review, among the women with an examination at 4 cm, 1.8% of the times from 4 cm to delivery
exceeded 24 hours and 0.2% exceeded 36 hours), so that a vaginal delivery is almost never truncated
and a caesarean section counts as at least as unfavourable as the longest labours ending in a
vaginal delivery. Beyond the vaginal deliveries, the horizon sets the weight given to a caesarean
section: with a mean time from 4 cm to vaginal delivery of about 8 hours, a difference of one
percentage point in caesarean sections changes the summary measure by about 0.3 hours. Horizons of
24 and 48 hours are supplementary analyses (@sec-supplementary-analyses).

There is no censoring: every woman is followed until delivery, whose time is recorded for all women
in the analysis set (it defines the time interval, @sec-analysis-sets). A caesarean section
contributes 36 hours whatever the time of reaching 4 cm, so time zero is needed only for vaginal
deliveries. Time zero is the vaginal examination at which 4 cm cervical dilatation was found. The
trial database records, for each centimetre, the time of the examination at which it was found, and
at the blinded review no examination found exactly 4 cm for 57% of the women (the first examination
at 4 cm or more found 5–10 cm), and about half of the women had no examination below 4 cm. For
women who deliver vaginally without an examination at 4 cm, the time of reaching 4 cm is multiply
imputed from a labour-curve model fitted to the vaginal deliveries. Following Zhang et al. (2002,
2010), who constructed labour curves from repeated cervical examinations with time measured
backwards from the end of labour because the onset of labour is poorly defined, the logarithm of
the time from each examination to delivery is modelled as a natural cubic spline of the dilatation
found (3 degrees of freedom), with a random intercept and slope per woman, fixed effects for
treatment, the interaction of treatment with dilatation, time interval, hospital and the covariates
of the primary endpoint, and a single residual variance. For each woman, the time of reaching 4 cm
is drawn from her predictive distribution given her own examinations, truncated to lie between her
last examination below 4 cm (if any) and her first examination at 4 cm or more, with the model
parameters drawn anew for each of 30 imputed datasets. A vaginal delivery more than 36 hours after
the observed or imputed time of reaching 4 cm contributes 36 hours. In a blinded validation of the
same imputation at 5 cm, which masked observed examinations, it removed most of the bias of taking
the first examination at or above the threshold as time zero (2.9–4.9 hours too short).

Because Y is known for every woman once time zero is imputed, the summary measure is estimated as a
difference in means, without a model for the distribution of the times. Y is analysed with a linear
mixed model with a random intercept for cluster and fixed effects for treatment, time interval and
the covariates of the primary endpoint (@sec-adjustment-for-covariates). With the identity link, the
treatment coefficient is the marginal difference in mean Y, and no G-computation is needed. Y is
not normally distributed (it has a point mass at 36 hours from the caesarean sections); the estimate
does not rely on normality, and with more than 30,000 women the confidence interval relies on the
central limit theorem. The model is fitted to each of the 30 imputed datasets, and the estimates and
their model-based variances are combined by Rubin's rules. The difference is presented with a
two-sided 95% confidence interval; no hypothesis test is performed (@sec-main-analytical-approach-for).

To show whether a difference comes from caesarean sections or from the duration of labour, two
components are presented: the difference in the probability of vaginal delivery, which is minus the
difference in caesarean sections in the primary analysis set including those at 4 cm
(supplementary analysis 1 of the primary estimand, @sec-supplementary-analysis), and the difference
in the mean of min(T, 36 h) among women who deliver vaginally, from the same model in the vaginal
delivery set. The latter conditions on vaginal delivery and is not interpreted as a treatment effect
on its own (@sec-estimands-for-secondary-objectives).

As supportive analyses, the cumulative incidence of vaginal delivery by time since 4 cm is shown for
each treatment (averaged over the imputed datasets; descriptive, not adjusted for time interval), and
the differences in the proportion of women delivered vaginally within 6 and within 12 hours of 4 cm
are estimated as for the dichotomous endpoints (@sec-main-analytical-approach-for) in each imputed
dataset and combined by Rubin's rules.

#### Sensitivity Analyses  {#sec-sensitivity-analyses-1}

<!-- COMMENT Stine Bernitz (2025-10-15): Are we sure? -->
<!-- COMMENT Inge Christoffer Olsen (2025-11-27): We can see once we start blindly anlaysing the data if we need some sensitivity analyses -->

For time from 4 cm cervical dilatation to vaginal delivery, two sensitivity analyses keep the
estimand and vary the model of @sec-main-analytical-approach-for-time-to:

1)  Unadjusted model: treatment, time interval and random cluster effect only.

2)  Fixed cluster effects with robust standard errors: hospital as a fixed effect instead of a random
    effect, with heteroscedasticity-consistent (HC3) standard errors, which do not assume a constant
    residual variance. The variance of Y depends strongly on the risk of caesarean section because of
    the point mass at 36 hours.

There will be no sensitivity analyses for the other secondary endpoints.

#### Supplementary Analyses  {#sec-supplementary-analyses}

For the endpoints analysed in the vaginal delivery set (occurrence of perineal support, episiotomy,
degree of perineal tears), a supplementary analysis uses a composite strategy in the primary
analysis set, counting a caesarean section as no event (no perineal support, no episiotomy, no
tear) (@sec-estimands-for-secondary-objectives).

For occurrence of amniotomy, use of oxytocin and use of epidural analgesia during labour,
supplementary analyses count any amniotomy, oxytocin infusion or epidural analgesia, whatever the
cervical dilatation at which it was performed or started, including amniotomy and oxytocin used for
induction of labour. These analyses include the women excluded from the main analysis because the
intervention was performed or started before 4 cm.

For time from 4 cm cervical dilatation to vaginal delivery, supplementary analyses restrict the time
without vaginal delivery to the first 24 and to the first 48 hours after 4 cm instead of 36 hours,
with the analysis of @sec-main-analytical-approach-for-time-to. The horizon sets the weight given to
a caesarean section, so each horizon defines a different estimand.

# Analyses Supporting Exploratory Objectives {#sec-analyses-supporting-exploratory}

Hypothesis generating exploratory analyses will be performed on exploratory endpoints. These
analyses will not be detailed in this analysis plan and will be regarded as post-hoc analyses.

Descriptive endpoint, especially categorical endpoints may be presented descriptively in the main
statistical report. The cervical dilatation at amniotomy, at the start of oxytocin infusion, at the
start of epidural analgesia and at induction of labour is presented as the number and percentage of
women by centimetre (1–10 cm, not recorded), by treatment
(@sec-definition-of-descriptive-or). Epidural analgesia is the only method of medical pain relief
with a recorded cervical dilatation.

The pre-specified subgroup analysis is described in @sec-subgroup-analyses.

## Subgroup Analyses {#sec-subgroup-analyses}

One exploratory subgroup analysis is prespecified, for the primary endpoint by Robson group (Ten
Group Classification System). The model of @sec-main-analytical-approach is extended with a
treatment × Robson group interaction, and the absolute risk difference is estimated within each
group by G-computation over the women of that group, with two-sided 95% confidence intervals
(delta method). Heterogeneity is assessed by a likelihood-ratio test of the interaction. Robson
groups with fewer than 50 intrapartum caesarean sections in the analysis set (both periods
together, known before unblinding) are combined into one group. The results are exploratory, not
adjusted for multiplicity, and no non-inferiority conclusion is drawn within subgroups.
Hospital-level characteristics (hospital, annual number of deliveries, intrapartum caesarean
section rate) are not used for subgroup analyses: with ten clusters, each subgroup would contain
only a few hospitals.

If there are indications of intervention-modifying baseline variables, further subgroup analyses may
be included as exploratory analyses.

# Interim Analyses {#sec-interim-analyses}

There will be no interim analyses.

# Changes to Protocol-planned Analyses {#sec-changes-to-protocol-planned-analyses}

<!-- COMMENT Inge Christoffer Olsen (2025-06-04): To be revised after we have finished the SAP -->

**Primary hypothesis.** The protocol describes a non-inferiority approach in its design section but
calculates the sample size for equivalence. This SAP specifies non-inferiority, with a margin of 1.5
percentage points for the absolute risk difference (@sec-statistical-hypotheses-and-conclusion). The
decision was made on 11 September 2026, before database lock and without access to unblinded data;
it does not reduce the power of the planned sample size (@sec-sample-size-determination).

# Sample Size Determination {#sec-sample-size-determination}

Our power calculation is based on the average rate of intrapartum caesarean section of 10.5 % in the
NORBIRTH network. If the 95% confidence interval of the difference in the proportions of caesarean
section between the LCG and the WHO partograph lies completely within -delta to +delta margins of
equivalence, then the two treatments are considered equivalent. With a power of 80%, a significance
level (alpha) of 5% and a delta margin of equivalence of ± 1.5 percentage points, the analysis need
to include 23 650 women considered the cluster effect and an estimated intraclass correlation
coefficient (ICC) of approximately 0.0001 as described by Henrichs et al. (19). Within the NORBIRTH
network approximately 28.950 women use a partograph each year. To secure a sufficient number of
individuals in the analyses, the inclusion period is estimated to last for one year and two months
(60 weeks). Each hospital will cross from WHO partograph to the LCG at equal time intervals until
all hospitals have crossed, which corresponds to five weeks per step taken into account a normal variation of annual deliveries and potential opt outs.

The primary hypothesis is non-inferiority (@sec-statistical-hypotheses-and-conclusion). The sample
size above was calculated for equivalence with the same margin, i.e. for two one-sided tests. The
non-inferiority test is one of these, so its power is at least that of the equivalence calculation,
and the trial is, if anything, over-powered for the non-inferiority claim. The number of women
included also exceeds the planned 23 650.

Derivation of covariates and baseline characteristics from the trial database (variable names as in
the data export). For multiple births, neonatal characteristics refer to the first-born twin.

| Characteristic | Source variable(s) | Derivation |
|----|----|----|
| Annual number of deliveries | `metadata/hospitals.csv` (births per year at the hospital) | 1000–1999, 2000–3999, ≥ 4000 |
| Contractions at admission | `antall_rier_10min_innkomst` | Number of contractions per 10 minutes at admission |
| Maternal age | `alder` | Age at the time of delivery in completed years (from date of birth), as recorded |
| Country of origin | `landbakgrunn` | Grouped by continent (country-to-continent lookup) |
| Married or cohabiting | `sivilstatus` | Married (`gift`) or cohabiting (`samboer`) vs other |
| Higher education | `utdanning` | University or college (`hoyere_utdanning`) vs lower |
| Height | `hoyde` | cm |
| Pre-pregnancy weight | `pregravid_vekt` | kg |
| Pre-pregnancy BMI | `hoyde`, `pregravid_vekt` | weight (kg) / height (m)^2^ |
| Smoking | `royk_for_eller_i_sv_s` | Smoking before or during pregnancy |
| Snuff use | `snus_for_eller_i_sv_s` | Snuff use before or during pregnancy |
| Medically treated diabetes | `hvilke_kjente_pregravide_sykdommer`, `hvilke_svangerskapsrelaterte_sykdommer` | Type 1 or type 2 diabetes, or gestational diabetes treated with metformin or insulin |
| Hypertensive disorders | as above | Chronic hypertension, gestational hypertension or pre-eclampsia |
| Robson group | `robson_gruppe` | As recorded (ten-group classification) |
| Parity | `paritet` | 0, 1, ≥ 2 |
| Previous caesarean section | `tidligere_sectio` | As recorded |
| First vaginal delivery | `paritet`, `tidligere_sectio` | Nulliparous, or para 1 with a previous caesarean section (para ≥ 2 with a previous caesarean section counted as no: not derivable) |
| Spontaneous onset of labour | `induksjon` | No induction (`induksjon` = 0) |
| Induction of labour | `induksjon` | `induksjon` = 1 |
| Gestational age | `gestasjonsalder_ved_fodsel_hele_uker`, `..._pluss_dager` | Weeks + days at birth |
| Sex of the baby | `barnets_kjonn` | As recorded |
| Birth weight | `fodselsvekt_gram` | g |
| Birthweight percentile | `fodselsvekt_gram`, gestational age, sex of the baby | Percentile for gestational age and sex; reference standard to be decided (INTERGROWTH-21st proposed) |
| Head circumference | `neonatal_hodeomkrets` | cm |
| Amniotomy before 4 cm | `amniotomi`, `cervix_apning_amniotomi` | Amniotomy at ≤ 3 cm cervical dilatation |
| Oxytocin started before 4 cm | `oxytocin_infusjon`, `cx_oppstart_oxytocin_infusjon` | Infusion started at ≤ 3 cm cervical dilatation |
| Epidural started before 4 cm | `type_medikamentell_smertelindring.epidural`, `cx_start_eda` | Epidural started at ≤ 3 cm cervical dilatation |
